data.label: Owner (@owner_sign)
data.description: Human owner of the AI agent
data.notes: The person who owns and controls the agent. Authenticates via atSign keypair stored in device keychain. Can interact via Flutter desktop/mobile app, or through messaging bridges (WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, iMessage). All commands are cryptographically signed with @owner_sign's private key so the agent can verify authenticity. Owner defines all policies, approves high-risk actions, and can revoke agent access at any time.

data.label: Flutter App (@owner_sign)
data.description: Cross-platform UI: chat, settings, policy editor, audit viewer
data.notes: Path: app/ | Entry: lib/main.dart | Cross-platform: macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android, Web | Features: Chat UI with streaming, Agent settings & policy editor, Skill marketplace browser with trust scores, Audit log viewer, Human-in-the-loop approval dialogs, Ollama-only privacy toggle | Auth: atSign keychain integration, no passwords | The app holds @owner_sign's atKeys and communicates exclusively through the atPlatform. Zero open ports on the owner's device.

data.label: Messaging Bridge (@bridge_sign)
data.description: WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, iMessage relay
data.notes: Path: bridge/ | Entry: bin/bridge.dart | Each bridge instance gets its own atSign (@bridge_whatsapp, @bridge_telegram, etc.) | Owner pairs each bridge by sharing @owner_sign. Bridge receives plaintext from chat platform, encrypts with @agent_sign's public key, and forwards via atPlatform. Responses are decrypted and relayed back to the chat platform. | CRITICAL: Bridge only relays — it never executes commands, accesses files, or stores context. It is a stateless encrypted relay. | Voice messages: Transcribed locally via Whisper before relay. | Security: Bridge atSigns have a 'relay-only' policy — the agent's policy engine verifies the originating @owner_sign on every message, not the bridge identity, preventing bridge impersonation.

data.label: atPlatform Network
data.description: E2E encrypted communication & identity layer
data.notes: Protocol: atProtocol over TCP/IP | Root server: root.atsign.org | All connections are OUTBOUND-ONLY from every component — no open inbound ports anywhere in the system. The atPlatform acts as a rendezvous point, not a data store. It facilitates key exchange and notification delivery but never sees plaintext data. | Key properties: Cryptographic identity verification before any connection | E2E encryption (AES-256 + RSA-2048) | No data retention on the platform itself | Namespace isolation between applications | Notification-based async messaging | Supports bind() for real-time streaming | Each atSign has a dedicated atServer (personal encrypted microservice) for storing its own data.

data.label: Agent Gateway (@agent_sign)
data.description: Secure entry point — auth, rate-limit, policy check
data.notes: Path: agent/bin/gateway.dart | The gateway is the ONLY entry point to the agent. It: 1) Receives encrypted notifications from atPlatform (outbound connection only) 2) Decrypts and verifies the sender's atSign identity 3) Checks the sender against the owner's allowlist policy 4) Rate-limits requests per sender 5) Routes verified commands to the Agent Orchestrator | CRITICAL DIFFERENCE FROM OPENCLAW: OpenClaw bound to 0.0.0.0:18789 with no auth. This gateway has ZERO open ports — it initiates an outbound connection to atPlatform and listens for notifications on that encrypted channel. Network scanners see nothing. | Binds to namespace: 'safeclaw.command.$agentSign' for incoming | Binds to namespace: 'safeclaw.response.$ownerSign' for outgoing

data.label: Agent Orchestrator
data.description: Core brain — query routing, planning, tool selection
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/core/orchestrator.dart | The orchestrator is the agent's decision-making core. Responsibilities: 1) Parse and classify incoming commands (chat, task, automation, skill invocation) 2) Privacy analysis — score query sensitivity (threshold: configurable, default 0.7) to decide local-only vs hybrid processing 3) Build execution plan — break complex tasks into steps with tool/skill requirements 4) Route each step to the appropriate executor (LLM Router, Skill Executor, MCP Client, or Automation Engine) 5) Aggregate results and stream response back through gateway 6) Log every decision and action to the Audit Service | Stateless design — all context loaded from Memory Service per request. Supports multi-turn conversations by loading relevant memory window.

data.label: Policy Engine
data.description: Dynamic access control — who can do what, when
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/core/policy_engine.dart | The policy engine enforces all access control decisions. It is consulted by the Gateway, Orchestrator, Skill Executor, and MCP Client before any action. | Policy types: 1) Identity policies — which atSigns can send commands (allowlist) 2) Capability policies — what each skill/tool can access (filesystem paths, network endpoints, shell commands) 3) Temporal policies — time-based access windows (e.g., no automated emails after 10pm) 4) Risk policies — actions requiring human-in-the-loop approval (financial transactions, sending emails, deleting files, external API calls above cost threshold) 5) Data policies — what data can leave the local system (privacy classification) | Policies are defined by owner via Flutter app or YAML config, stored encrypted on @agent_sign's atServer. | CRITICAL: Policies are enforced at the infrastructure level by atPlatform, not just in application code. A compromised skill cannot bypass the policy engine because the atPlatform itself restricts the skill's atSign permissions.

data.label: LLM Router
data.description: Routes queries to local or external LLMs based on privacy score
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/services/llm_router.dart | Decision logic: 1) If privacy_score >= threshold OR owner set 'local-only' mode → route to Local LLM (Ollama) 2) If privacy_score < threshold AND query needs external knowledge → sanitize via Sanitizer, then route to External LLM 3) If hybrid mode → local LLM processes with full context, external LLM provides supplementary knowledge on sanitized sub-query, results merged locally | The router NEVER sends raw user context to external LLMs. The Sanitizer strips all personal identifiers, locations, names, account numbers, and conversation history before any external call. | Supports model selection: owner can configure which local model (llama3.2, mistral, phi-3, deepseek, etc.) and which external provider (Claude, GPT, Gemini, or none).

data.label: Local LLM (Ollama)
data.description: On-device inference — handles 90%+ of queries
data.notes: Host: http://localhost:11434 (loopback only, never exposed) | Docker: ollama/ollama with --network=none option for air-gapped mode | Configurable models: llama3.2, mistral, phi-3, deepseek-coder, gemma2, codellama, or any GGUF model | Handles ALL queries in local-only mode, and all privacy-sensitive queries in hybrid mode | Full context access: conversation history, user preferences, personal data — because nothing leaves the device | Also used for: privacy scoring (classify query sensitivity), query sanitization (identify PII to strip), and skill output validation (check results before presenting to user) | GPU acceleration: CUDA, ROCm, Metal supported | Fallback: CPU inference if no GPU available

data.label: Query Sanitizer
data.description: Strips PII before any external API call
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/services/sanitizer.dart | Uses local LLM to identify and remove: names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, account numbers, locations, dates of birth, IP addresses, and any owner-defined sensitive patterns | Produces a sanitized query that preserves the intent but contains zero personal data | Also sanitizes tool/skill outputs before they reach external LLMs | Reversible mapping: maintains a local-only lookup table so the orchestrator can re-inject context into the external LLM's response before presenting to user | The sanitizer itself NEVER makes external calls — it runs entirely on the local LLM

data.label: External LLM (Optional)
data.description: Claude, GPT, Gemini — only receives sanitized queries
data.notes: Configurable provider: Claude API (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929), OpenAI (gpt-4o), Google (gemini-2.0-flash), or NONE (fully local mode) | API keys stored encrypted on @agent_sign's atServer — never in plaintext .env files | Only receives sanitized queries — no personal data, no conversation history, no user context | Used for: current events, specialized knowledge, complex reasoning that exceeds local model capabilities | The external LLM has NO knowledge of the user's identity, location, or personal information | Rate-limited by policy engine to control cost | Owner can disable entirely via 'local-only' toggle in Flutter app

data.label: Memory Service (@agent_sign)
data.description: Encrypted persistent memory with source tagging
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/services/memory_service.dart | Storage: All memory stored encrypted on @agent_sign's atServer using atClient.put() | Memory types: 1) Conversation history — full chat logs with TTL (configurable, default 90 days) 2) User context — preferences, habits, personal info (owner-managed) 3) Task memory — ongoing automations, scheduled jobs, reminders 4) Skill memory — per-skill state, sandboxed (skill A cannot read skill B's memory) | CRITICAL SECURITY: Every memory entry is tagged with: source_atsign (who created it), trust_level (owner, verified_skill, unverified_input, external_llm), timestamp, and content_hash | Memory from untrusted sources (web results, forwarded messages, external LLM responses) is stored with trust_level='unverified_input' and CANNOT escalate to command authority even after extended time in memory. This prevents the delayed multi-turn memory poisoning attacks that plague OpenClaw. | The local LLM periodically summarizes and compacts old memory to manage context window limits.

data.label: Audit Service
data.description: Tamper-proof log of every agent action
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/services/audit_service.dart | Every action the agent takes is logged with: timestamp, action_type, initiator_atsign, target_resource, policy_decision (allowed/denied/escalated), input_hash, output_hash, execution_duration | Logs are cryptographically signed with @agent_sign's private key and stored on the owner's atServer | Logs CANNOT be modified by the agent, a compromised skill, or an attacker — the atServer enforces append-only semantics for audit namespace | Owner can query, filter, and export logs via Flutter app | Alerting: Policy violations, unusual patterns (sudden spike in file access, unexpected network calls), and failed auth attempts trigger real-time notifications to @owner_sign | Integration: Logs can be forwarded to external SIEM/SOC systems via a dedicated export atSign with read-only access

data.description: Owner types command or query in chat UI. Authentication is automatic via atSign keychain — no passwords.
Owner sends command via WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, or iMessage. Bridge encrypts and relays.
Bridge encrypts message with @agent_sign's public key. Includes @owner_sign verification signature. Bridge never stores or processes the command content.
Query encrypted with @agent_sign's public key. Sent via atPlatform notification to namespace 'safeclaw.command.$agentSign'. No open ports needed — outbound connection only.
atPlatform delivers encrypted notification to the agent's outbound connection. Gateway decrypts with @agent_sign's private key, verifies sender identity.
Gateway asks policy engine: Is this sender (@owner_sign) on the allowlist? Is this command type permitted at this time? Rate limit check.
Only after policy engine approves: decrypted, identity-verified command is passed to the orchestrator with the sender's trust level attached.
Orchestrator sends query with full user context and privacy score to LLM Router for inference routing.
Full context query routed to local Ollama instance. No data leaves the device. POST to localhost:11434/api/generate with streaming.
Only when local LLM cannot answer (current events, specialized knowledge) AND privacy score allows. Query sent to sanitizer first — NEVER directly to external LLM.

All PII, personal context, names, locations, and identifiers stripped. External LLM receives a generic knowledge query with zero user information. API key retrieved from encrypted atServer, never stored in plaintext files.
Orchestrator streams assembled response back through gateway. Batched: 500ms or 50 chars, whichever comes first.
Response encrypted with @owner_sign's public key. Streamed via atPlatform notification to 'safeclaw.response.$ownerSign'.
Real-time streaming via bind() listener on the app. User sees response tokens appear as they are generated.
Owner sees streaming response in chat UI. Throttled UI rebuild at 100ms intervals for smooth rendering.
Load conversation history and user context at request start. Save new exchanges with source tags and trust levels after completion.
Every decision, tool invocation, LLM call, and response is logged with cryptographic signature. Append-only, tamper-proof.
Before executing any tool, skill, or risky action, the orchestrator checks with the policy engine. Denied actions are logged and the owner is notified.

data.label: Agent Orchestrator
data.description: Routes tasks to appropriate skill executors
data.notes: When a command requires a skill (e.g., 'check my calendar', 'organize my photos', 'book a flight'), the orchestrator: 1) Identifies the required skill 2) Checks the skill's trust level and declared capabilities against the policy engine 3) Provisions a sandboxed execution environment 4) Passes the task with ONLY the data the skill is authorized to access 5) Monitors execution and enforces time limits 6) Validates output before returning to user

data.label: Skill Registry (@agent_sign)
data.description: Local catalog of installed skills with trust metadata
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/skills/registry.dart | Each installed skill entry contains: skill_id, skill_atsign (@skill_calendar, @skill_email, etc.), developer_atsign (who published it), signature_hash (cryptographic signature of the skill package), declared_capabilities (list of resources it needs: filesystem paths, network endpoints, APIs), trust_score (computed from: developer reputation, audit history, community reviews, certification status), installed_version, and policy_overrides (owner's custom restrictions) | Skills are discovered via the Skill Marketplace but installed locally. The registry verifies the developer's atSign signature before installation. | CRITICAL DIFFERENCE FROM OPENCLAW's ClawHub: Every skill has a verified developer identity (atSign). Unsigned or tampered skills are rejected at install time. No anonymous skill publishing.

data.label: Skill Marketplace
data.description: Community skill catalog with verified developer identities
data.notes: A public registry where developers publish skills. Each skill listing includes: developer atSign (verified identity), capability declaration (what resources the skill needs), source code hash, automated security scan results (static analysis, dependency audit, sandbox escape detection), community trust score (usage count, reviews, issue reports), and certification status (Atsign-audited or community-reviewed). | Unlike OpenClaw's ClawHub where Paul McCarty found 386 malicious packages in minutes, this marketplace: 1) Requires developer identity via atSign (no anonymous publishing) 2) Runs automated security scanning before listing 3) Sandboxes all skills by default — even if malicious code exists, it cannot escape the sandbox 4) Provides transparent audit trails per developer | Skill packages are signed with the developer's atSign private key. The agent verifies this signature at install time.

data.label: Sandbox Manager
data.description: Creates isolated execution environments per skill invocation
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/skills/sandbox_manager.dart | For each skill invocation, the sandbox manager: 1) Spins up an ephemeral container (Docker/Firecracker microVM) or OS-level sandbox (seccomp + namespaces on Linux, Sandbox on macOS) 2) Mounts ONLY the directories the skill declared AND the owner approved — read-only by default 3) Sets network policy: most skills get --network=none. Skills that need network (e.g., web search) get allowlisted endpoints only 4) Injects the skill's atSign credentials for atPlatform communication (scoped to skill's namespace only) 5) Sets resource limits: CPU time, memory, disk I/O 6) Monitors for sandbox escape attempts and terminates immediately if detected | After execution, the sandbox is destroyed. No persistent state outside the skill's designated atServer namespace.

data.label: Calendar Skill (@skill_cal)
data.description: Example: reads/writes calendar entries only
data.notes: Declared capabilities: read/write to 'calendar.*' namespace on owner's atServer | No filesystem access, no network access, no shell execution | Runs in sandbox with --network=none | Can only communicate via atPlatform within its declared namespace | If it attempts to read email namespace or access filesystem → sandbox blocks + audit alert to owner | Example invocation: 'Schedule a meeting with Bob tomorrow at 3pm' → Orchestrator passes only the scheduling request, not the full conversation history

data.label: Email Skill (@skill_email)
data.description: Example: draft and send emails with human approval
data.notes: Declared capabilities: read/write to 'email.*' namespace, network access to SMTP endpoint only | REQUIRES human-in-the-loop: every outbound email must be approved by owner via Flutter app notification before sending | Runs in sandbox with network allowlist: only the configured SMTP server | Cannot read calendar, filesystem, or other skill namespaces | The skill drafts the email and stores it in 'email.draft' namespace. The policy engine holds it for owner approval. Only after owner confirms does the skill get temporary send permission. | This prevents the OpenClaw attack vector where a prompt injection could silently send emails containing stolen data

data.label: File Organizer Skill (@skill_files)
data.description: Example: organize files in designated directories only
data.notes: Declared capabilities: read/write to owner-specified directories only (e.g., ~/Documents/ToOrganize) | No network access (--network=none), no shell execution, no access to ~/.ssh, ~/.config, or any directory outside the declared scope | Cannot read other skills' data, cannot access browser profiles, cannot touch API keys or credentials | Sandbox mounts the target directory as the only writable volume | CRITICAL: Unlike OpenClaw where file access = full homedir access, this skill can only touch what the owner explicitly designated. Even if the skill's code is malicious, it cannot read SSH keys, browser cookies, or password vaults.

data.label: Policy Engine
data.description: Validates skill capabilities against owner-defined policies
data.notes: Before any skill executes, the policy engine: 1) Compares the skill's declared capabilities against the owner's approved capabilities for that skill 2) Checks temporal restrictions (is this skill allowed to run right now?) 3) Determines if human-in-the-loop is required (based on action type and risk level) 4) If the skill attempts to exceed its declared capabilities at runtime, the sandbox blocks the attempt and the policy engine logs a violation + alerts the owner | Owner can adjust policies per-skill via the Flutter app: grant more access, restrict further, or revoke entirely

data.label: Audit Service
data.description: Logs every skill invocation, capability check, and sandbox event
data.notes: Records per skill invocation: skill_atsign, invocation_timestamp, input_data_hash (what data was passed in), capabilities_used (what the skill actually accessed), capabilities_denied (what the sandbox blocked), output_data_hash, execution_time, sandbox_events (any escape attempts, resource limit hits), policy_decisions | All entries signed and append-only

data.description: Orchestrator queries registry: Is the required skill installed? What is its trust score? What capabilities does it declare?
If skill not installed or update available: download from marketplace, verify developer atSign signature, run security scan, register locally.
Orchestrator requests a sandboxed execution environment with the skill's declared (and owner-approved) capabilities.
Before creating the sandbox, confirm all requested capabilities are approved by the owner's policy.
Skill runs inside ephemeral sandbox with only calendar namespace access. Destroyed after completion.
Email skill runs in sandbox, drafts email, then PAUSES for human-in-the-loop owner approval before sending.
File skill runs with single-directory mount. Cannot see or touch anything outside its designated folder.
Every sandbox lifecycle event is logged: creation, capability grants, runtime access attempts, completion or termination, resource usage.
Every policy allow/deny/escalate decision is logged with the requesting skill's atSign and the rule that matched.

data.label: Agent Orchestrator
data.description: Routes tool calls to secure MCP client
data.notes: When the agent needs to interact with external tools and APIs (databases, SaaS platforms, home automation, etc.), it does so through MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers — but secured via atPlatform. The orchestrator never connects to MCP servers directly. All connections go through the Secure MCP Client which wraps every MCP channel in atPlatform encryption.

data.label: Secure MCP Client (@agent_sign)
data.description: atPlatform-wrapped MCP connections — no open ports, no exposed APIs
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/mcp/secure_mcp_client.dart | This is the CRITICAL security layer that addresses the MCP Security Paradox (43% of MCP implementations have command injection flaws). | How it works: 1) Each MCP server the agent connects to must have its own atSign (@mcp_homeassistant, @mcp_postgres, @mcp_gmail, etc.) 2) The MCP client establishes an atPlatform E2E encrypted channel to each MCP server's atSign 3) MCP tool calls and responses flow through this encrypted tunnel — never over raw HTTP/stdio/SSE 4) The atPlatform verifies both identities (agent atSign ↔ MCP server atSign) before any connection 5) No open ports on either side — both agent and MCP server use outbound-only connections to atPlatform | Tool calls are further filtered by the policy engine: the agent can only invoke tools that the owner has explicitly approved for each MCP server. | This eliminates the Shadow IT problem where developers spin up unprotected local MCP servers with root-level access.

data.label: Context-Aware Tool Filter
data.description: Dynamic tool exposure based on agent identity and task context
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/mcp/tool_filter.dart | Implements context-aware tool exposure as described in the atPlatform architecture: 1) Each MCP server defines a full list of available tools 2) The tool filter dynamically restricts which tools the agent can see based on: the current task type, the owner's policies, the trust level of the original request source, and temporal rules 3) Example: An MCP server connected to a CRM might expose both 'read_contact' and 'delete_contact'. The tool filter ensures the agent only sees 'read_contact' unless the owner has specifically granted delete permissions for the current task. | This prevents the confused deputy problem: even if the agent is tricked by a prompt injection into attempting a dangerous action, the tool filter has already hidden the dangerous tools from the agent's available options.

data.label: atPlatform Network
data.description: Encrypted tunnel between agent and MCP servers
data.notes: All MCP traffic flows through atPlatform's E2E encrypted channels. The atPlatform: 1) Verifies both identities cryptographically before allowing any connection 2) Encrypts all tool calls and responses end-to-end 3) Enforces namespace isolation — MCP server A cannot see traffic intended for MCP server B 4) Provides no-port connectivity: both the agent and MCP servers connect outbound to atPlatform, so neither exposes any inbound ports | This directly addresses Akamai's finding that network exposure without authentication was OpenClaw's primary breach vector.

data.label: Home Automation MCP (@mcp_home)
data.description: Controls smart home devices via Home Assistant
data.notes: Runs alongside Home Assistant on the home server | Has its own atSign: @mcp_home | Outbound-only connection to atPlatform — no port forwarding, no exposed Home Assistant API | Available tools: lights_control, thermostat_set, lock_status, camera_snapshot | Policy restrictions: lock_control requires HITL approval, camera access logged to audit | The MCP server itself runs NoPorts (Atsign's zero-port connectivity tool) so the home server has ZERO open inbound ports

data.label: Database MCP (@mcp_db)
data.description: Secure access to personal or work databases
data.notes: Wraps PostgreSQL, SQLite, or any database with atPlatform security | Has its own atSign: @mcp_db | Available tools: query_read, query_write, schema_inspect | Policy restrictions: query_write requires HITL approval for DELETE/DROP operations. query_read is limited to owner-specified tables/views — no SELECT * FROM pg_shadow. | All queries are parameterized — the MCP server rejects raw SQL string concatenation | Rate limited: max 100 queries/hour by default | No open ports — database is only accessible through the atPlatform encrypted tunnel, never exposed to the network

data.label: Web Browser MCP (@mcp_browser)
data.description: Controlled web browsing with content sanitization
data.notes: Provides agent with web browsing capabilities — but sandboxed | Has its own atSign: @mcp_browser | Available tools: navigate_url, extract_text, fill_form, take_screenshot | CRITICAL SECURITY: 1) Runs in a separate browser profile — no access to owner's cookies, saved passwords, or browsing history 2) Content from web pages is treated as UNTRUSTED INPUT with trust_level='unverified_input' — it cannot become command-authority in memory 3) fill_form requires HITL approval (prevents unauthorized purchases, account changes) 4) URL allowlist: owner can restrict browsing to approved domains 5) Content is passed through the sanitizer before reaching the LLM to strip potential prompt injection payloads embedded in web pages | This directly addresses Palo Alto's finding about indirect prompt injection via web content in OpenClaw

data.label: Policy Engine
data.description: Controls which MCP tools are available and when
data.notes: For MCP connections, the policy engine manages: 1) Which MCP servers the agent is allowed to connect to (allowlist of @mcp_* atSigns) 2) Which tools on each server are exposed to the agent (context-aware tool filter rules) 3) Which tools require human-in-the-loop approval 4) Rate limits per MCP server 5) Temporal restrictions (e.g., no home automation control between 11pm-6am unless emergency) 6) Data flow restrictions (e.g., data from @mcp_db cannot be forwarded to external LLM)

data.description: Orchestrator requests a specific tool call on a specific MCP server. Request includes task context for the tool filter.
Before invoking any tool, the client checks the filter: Is this tool visible to the agent for this task? Is the action within the declared scope?
Tool filter consults policy engine for current permissions, HITL requirements, and rate limits.
Approved tool call is encrypted with the target MCP server's atSign public key and sent through atPlatform. No open ports on either side.
Home automation MCP server receives tool call via outbound-only atPlatform connection. Decrypts, executes against Home Assistant, encrypts response.
Database MCP server receives parameterized query via encrypted tunnel. No raw SQL passthrough. Results encrypted back to agent.
Browser MCP operates in isolated profile. Web content flagged as untrusted. Form fills require HITL approval.
Before routing to MCP client, orchestrator confirms the target MCP server is on the allowlist and the action type is permitted.

data.label: Agent Orchestrator
data.description: Manages scheduled tasks and proactive automations
data.notes: Beyond responding to user commands, the agent runs a heartbeat loop for proactive task execution. This is where the 'always-on assistant' capability lives — analogous to OpenClaw's cron-style automations, but secured with policy enforcement and audit logging at every step.

data.label: Task Scheduler
data.description: Cron-like scheduling with policy-gated execution
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/automation/scheduler.dart | Manages recurring and one-time scheduled tasks. Each task entry: task_id, schedule (cron expression), skill_to_invoke, parameters, policy_requirements (HITL needed?), max_retries, owner_atsign (who created it) | Examples: 'Every morning at 7am, summarize overnight emails' → invokes Email Skill (read) + LLM Router | 'Every Friday at 5pm, generate weekly expense report' → invokes Database MCP + File Skill | 'In 2 hours, remind me to call Bob' → simple notification | CRITICAL: Every scheduled execution goes through the SAME policy engine check as interactive commands. A scheduled task cannot bypass HITL requirements or capability restrictions. | Owner can view, modify, pause, and delete all scheduled tasks via Flutter app.

data.label: Heartbeat Engine
data.description: Periodic proactive checks — configurable cadence
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/automation/heartbeat.dart | Runs at a configurable interval (default: 30 minutes, like OpenClaw's heartbeat) | Each heartbeat cycle: 1) Check for pending scheduled tasks 2) Check for new notifications/messages across connected platforms 3) Run proactive checks the owner has configured (e.g., 'alert me if any email from $domain arrives', 'notify me if stock $TICKER drops below $X') 4) Run memory maintenance (summarize old conversations, compact context) 5) Run system health checks (LLM availability, MCP server connectivity) | Each heartbeat action is logged to audit. Proactive notifications to the owner are sent via atPlatform encrypted channel. | Owner can adjust cadence per automation type: email checks every 10 mins, stock checks every 5 mins, memory maintenance daily.

data.label: Notification Manager
data.description: Routes proactive alerts to owner via encrypted channels
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/automation/notification_manager.dart | When the agent needs to proactively notify the owner (scheduled task results, alerts, approval requests), the notification manager: 1) Formats the notification with context and urgency level 2) Encrypts with @owner_sign's public key 3) Sends via atPlatform to the owner's preferred channel (Flutter app push notification, or relayed to messaging bridge) | Urgency levels: LOW (batched into daily digest), MEDIUM (delivered immediately), HIGH (delivered immediately with repeat until acknowledged), CRITICAL (all channels simultaneously) | HITL approval requests are always HIGH urgency with a timeout — if the owner doesn't respond within the configured window, the action is DENIED by default (fail-closed).

data.label: Human-in-the-Loop Manager
data.description: Queues and manages actions awaiting owner approval
data.notes: Path: agent/lib/automation/hitl_manager.dart | When the policy engine flags an action as requiring human approval: 1) The HITL manager stores the pending action with full context (what skill, what it wants to do, what data it will access, why) 2) Sends an approval request to the owner via notification manager 3) The owner sees a rich approval dialog in the Flutter app: action description, risk assessment, and approve/deny/modify buttons 4) If approved: the original action is executed with a time-limited permission grant 5) If denied: the action is cancelled and the skill is informed 6) If timeout: the action is DENIED (fail-closed) and owner is informed | Examples of HITL actions: sending emails, making purchases, modifying files outside sandbox, DELETE database queries, accessing new MCP servers for the first time, installing new skills | The approval itself is cryptographically signed by @owner_sign — a compromised agent cannot forge an approval.

data.label: Policy Engine
data.description: Same policy enforcement for automated and interactive actions
data.notes: Automated and scheduled tasks receive IDENTICAL policy scrutiny as interactive user commands. There is no 'background mode' that bypasses security. The policy engine checks every heartbeat-triggered and scheduler-triggered action before execution.

data.label: Audit Service
data.description: Logs all automation events, scheduled task executions, and HITL decisions
data.notes: Records: scheduler fire events, heartbeat cycle summaries, notification deliveries, HITL request/response pairs (including timeout-denials), proactive action outcomes. All signed and append-only.

data.description: Owner commands like 'remind me every Monday' or 'check my email every 10 minutes' create scheduler entries.
Continuous heartbeat cycle: check scheduler, process notifications, run proactive checks, maintain memory.
Every scheduled task execution is policy-checked. No bypass for automated actions.
Proactive heartbeat actions are policy-checked identically to interactive commands.
Policy engine flags high-risk actions for human-in-the-loop approval. Action is paused until owner decides.
HITL manager sends rich approval request to owner. Includes full action context, risk assessment, and approve/deny options.
Heartbeat check results that match owner's alert conditions are sent as proactive notifications.
Every scheduled task execution and its outcome is logged.
Every HITL request, owner response (approve/deny/timeout), and resulting action is logged with cryptographic signatures.

data.label: Local Deployment (Recommended)
data.description: Agent runs on owner's hardware — maximum privacy
data.notes: Deploy on: Mac Mini, Linux server, Raspberry Pi 5, Windows PC, or any Docker-capable host | Components: 1) Agent Gateway + Orchestrator + Policy Engine (single Dart binary) 2) Ollama (local LLM, Docker or native) 3) MCP servers (containerized, one per service) 4) atServer (auto-provisioned per atSign) | ALL connections are OUTBOUND-ONLY to atPlatform. The host machine has ZERO open inbound ports. Network scanners see nothing. data.label: Security Comparison: OpenClaw vs SafeClaw (atPlatform)
data.description: Side-by-side vulnerability analysis
data.notes:
This comparison maps every major OpenClaw vulnerability to the corresponding SafeClaw mitigation:

1) NETWORK EXPOSURE
   OpenClaw: Bound to 0.0.0.0:18789, no auth. 30K+ instances exposed.
   SafeClaw: Zero open ports. Outbound-only atPlatform connections. Invisible to scanners.

2) AUTHENTICATION
   OpenClaw: No auth by default. Anyone on the network can send commands.
   SafeClaw: Cryptographic identity verification (atSign keypairs) required before any connection. No passwords.

3) CREDENTIALS
   OpenClaw: Plaintext API keys in ~/.clawdbot/.env and clawdbot.json.
   SafeClaw: All secrets encrypted on atServer. Retrieved via atSDK at runtime, never written to disk in plaintext.

4) SKILL/PLUGIN SECURITY
   OpenClaw: ClawHub had 386 malicious packages. Skills run with full agent permissions.
   SafeClaw: Verified developer identity (atSign). Skills declare capabilities upfront. Sandboxed execution. Skills cannot exceed declared permissions.

5) PROMPT INJECTION
   OpenClaw: Web content and messages processed with full agent authority.
   SafeClaw: All untrusted input tagged with source identity and trust level. Untrusted content processed in restricted context. Cannot escalate to command authority.

6) MEMORY POISONING
   OpenClaw: Persistent memory treats all inputs equally. Delayed attack chains possible.
   SafeClaw: Memory entries tagged with source atSign and trust level. Untrusted memory cannot become commands even over time.

7) CONFUSED DEPUTY
   OpenClaw: Agent can be tricked into misusing tools it has access to.
   SafeClaw: Context-aware tool filtering hides dangerous tools from the agent unless explicitly needed. Policy enforced at atPlatform level, not application code.

8) SUPPLY CHAIN
   OpenClaw: Skills marketplace flooded with malware within days.
   SafeClaw: Developer identity via atSign. Signed packages. Automated security scanning. Sandboxed execution even if malicious code exists.

9) LATERAL MOVEMENT
   OpenClaw: Full user-level filesystem, network, and shell access.
   SafeClaw: Picosegmented access per skill/tool. Each component can only touch its declared resources.

10) AUDIT
    OpenClaw: No audit trail. Breaches undetected until credentials weaponized.
    SafeClaw: Cryptographically signed, append-only audit log of every action. Real-time alerts on policy violations.

data.description: All atSigns needed for a complete deployment
Local deployment inherits all atPlatform security properties: zero open ports, cryptographic auth, E2E encryption.
Cloud deployment has identical security posture: zero open ports, invisible to scanners, no admin panels exposed. Unlike OpenClaw's 30K exposed cloud instances.
Every security improvement in the comparison is rooted in the atSign identity model. Each component gets a unique, cryptographically verifiable identity.
